strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing practical challenges in RL-based report generation: The paper clearly identifies two major failure modes of policy optimization with KL regularization—namely, the inflexibility of a fixed KL coefficient across diverse responses, and the accumulation of KL pressure against a static reference policy leading to exploration stifling or training collapse.

Technically sound and elegant formulation: Response-Weighted Regularization (RER) cleverly utilizes reference policy entropy and advantage sign to adaptively relax constraints on promising exploratory responses while penalizing harmful deviations. Complementarily, Validation-Anchored Policy Reset (VAPR) provides an intuitive, empirically grounded way to reset the reference anchor to the best validation checkpoint, avoiding drift and reward hacking associated with moving-average updates.

Comprehensive empirical validation: REVA-PO demonstrates consistent performance gains across both linguistic (NLG) and clinical efficacy (CE) metrics on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray. Ablation studies thoroughly dissect the individual contributions of each stage in the three-stage pipeline as well as the RL components (RER and VAPR).

Insightful reward analysis: The supplementary analysis (Appendix A) provides convincing empirical reasoning (reward variance and reward inversion / entity stuffing) justifying why BLEU-4 acts as a more robust surrogate reward than direct clinical metrics like CheXpert F1 or RadGraph F1.
weaknesses: Potential confounding from stronger LVLM backbone: The proposed approach adopts Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, a very recent and highly capable vision-language model, whereas most prior benchmarks in Table 1 rely on older or smaller backbones (e.g., Llama-2-7B, GPT-2, or custom vision-language encoders). Although the ablation studies in Tables 3 and 4 clearly validate the incremental contributions under the same model, directly evaluating existing baseline methods (e.g., standard GRPO or PromptMRG) under the exact same Qwen2.5-VL backbone would make the comparative SOTA claims even more definitive.

Subsampling in Stage 3: Due to compute constraints, Stage 3 RL is conducted on a 10k subset of MIMIC-CXR rather than the full training set. While understandable given compute limitations, it leaves open whether the policy stability and convergence behavior of REVA-PO vs. baselines persist when scaling to the entire dataset.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: VAPR introduces additional hyperparameters, notably the validation reset period (M = 3 epochs) and metric balancing factor lambda. The manuscript would benefit from a sensitivity analysis regarding how frequently VAPR resets should occur relative to policy update frequency.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-identified and important challenge in reinforcement learning for vision-language generation: balancing exploration and policy collapse caused by rigid KL regularization and static reference policies.

The proposed Response-Weighted Regularization (RER) is lightweight and critic-free, elegantly utilizing reference-policy sequence entropy and advantage to modulate regularizer strength at the response level.

Validation-Anchored Policy Reset (VAPR) provides a simple yet effective mechanism to alleviate accumulated KL pressure by periodically resetting policies to the best-validated checkpoint, avoiding the lag and reward-hacking risks inherent in EMA tracking.

The empirical results on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray are strong, consistently outperforming existing methods on both standard natural language generation (NLG) and clinical efficacy (CE) metrics (CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1).

The paper and supplementary material provide thoughtful analyses, particularly regarding why BLEU-4 serves as a robust proxy reward compared to CheXpert F1 (due to high variance) and RadGraph F1 (due to reward inversion and entity stuffing).
weaknesses: The RL phase optimizes exclusively for BLEU-4 (an n-gram lexical overlap metric). Although the authors demonstrate a positive correlation between BLEU-4 advantage and CheXpert F1 advantage, direct optimization for clinical correctness without relying solely on lexical proxies or exploring hybrid rewards remains an open question.

The framework relies heavily on an external classifier (Medical MAE) to inject predicted CheXpert labels into the prompt in Stage 2 and 3. While Table 3 shows Stage 3 RL yields further improvements over Stage 2 SFT, decoupling the contribution of classifier cues from the LVLM's intrinsic visual understanding deserves deeper discussion.

The piecewise linear formulation in Eq. (9) introduces several hyperparameters (\beta_{min}, \beta_{base}, \beta_{max}). The manuscript lacks a thorough sensitivity analysis evaluating how sensitive model stability and performance are to variations in these bounds.

The validation of REVA-PO as a general RL optimization algorithm is restricted to chest X-ray report generation; evaluating its effectiveness on broader vision-language reasoning or instruction-following benchmarks would strengthen the algorithmic claims.

strengths: Well-motivated RL stabilization framework: The paper tackles two well-known failure modes of RL in text and vision-language generation—the rigidity of fixed KL penalties across diverse response qualities, and the accumulation of KL pressure against a static reference policy leading to policy collapse. The proposed Response-Weighted Regularization (RER) and Validation-Anchored Policy Reset (VAPR) offer elegant, practical solutions.

Comprehensive empirical gains: REVA-PO demonstrates consistent and noticeable improvements across both linguistic (BLEU, ROUGE-L) and clinical efficacy metrics (CheXpert F1, RadGraph F1) on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, outperforming recent LLM and non-LLM baselines.

Detailed ablation and stability analysis: The ablation experiments (Tables 3 & 4 and Figure 3) clearly validate the necessity of each stage in the three-stage pipeline, the sample efficiency provided by RER over constant KL, and the prevention of training collapse enabled by VAPR.

Insightful reward dynamics discussion: Supplementary Material A provides valuable empirical analysis on the perils of directly optimizing clinical metrics like CheXpert F1 (due to high group variance) and RadGraph F1 (due to reward inversion and entity-stuffing vulnerabilities), justifying why BLEU-4 serves as a more stable proxy reward.

High clarity and reproducibility: The pipeline and algorithm are presented clearly with full hyperparameter details, prompt templates, and computational overhead profiling provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Backbone confounding factor: The base model employed is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, a significantly newer and stronger multimodal foundation model than those utilized by many compared baselines (e.g., LLaMA-2-7B, GPT-2, or domain-specific older transformers). While Table 4 demonstrates the value of RER and VAPR over constant KL on the same architecture, having baseline RLHF/GRPO or DPO methods evaluated on the exact same Qwen2.5-VL backbone would provide a clearer isolation of the RL algorithmic gains from the base model's capabilities.

Heuristic hyperparameter formulation: The mapping from normalized reference entropy to response-level KL weight in Eq. (9) introduces several hand-tuned bounds (\beta_{min}, \beta_{base}, \beta_{max}), alongside reset intervals M and N. A broader sensitivity analysis across these hyperparameters would strengthen confidence in their robustness across other models and tasks.

Lack of expert human evaluation: In medical report generation, automated metrics (CheXpert labeler, RadGraph F1) can miss subtle diagnostic errors, misattributions, or clinical flow issues. A blinded evaluation by certified radiologists comparing REVA-PO against human reference reports and baseline outputs would make the clinical impact claims significantly stronger.
